title: Circle Theorems: Secrets of the Ring

blocks.title: 1. The Core Concept: Hidden Rules Inside Circles
blocks.content: A circle looks simple, but it hides some of the most elegant rules in geometry. When you draw lines inside a circle (chords, tangents, diameters), they create angles that follow strict, beautiful patterns. These **Circle Theorems** let you find unknown angles instantly, without needing a protractor. They're the cheat codes of geometry exams.

blocks.title: 2. The Rules: The Big Five Theorems
blocks.content:
• **Theorem 1:** The angle at the center is TWICE the angle at the circumference (from the same arc).
• **Theorem 2:** Angles in the same segment are equal.
• **Theorem 3:** The angle in a semicircle is always 90 degrees (if the chord is a diameter).
• **Theorem 4:** Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees.
• **Theorem 5:** A tangent to a circle meets the radius at exactly 90 degrees.

blocks.title: 3. Step-by-Step: Identifying Which Theorem to Use
blocks.content:
When faced with a circle diagram:

1. Look for the **center point**. If angles are drawn from it, use Theorem 1.
2. Look for a **diameter** (line through the center). Any angle touching the opposite circumference = 90.
3. Look for a **tangent** (line touching the circle once). It makes 90 with the radius.
4. Look for a **cyclic quad** (4 points on the circle). Opposite angles = 180.
5. Always mark the known angles and work outward.

blocks.title: 4. Worked Example: Angle at the Center
blocks.content:
The angle at the center of a circle is 140 degrees. Find the angle at the circumference from the same arc.

**Step 1:** Identify: We have a center angle and need the circumference angle from the same arc.
**Step 2:** Apply Theorem 1: Center angle = 2 x Circumference angle.
**Step 3:** 140 = 2 x Circumference angle.
**Step 4:** Circumference angle = 140 / 2 = 70.

**Final Answer: 70 degrees.**

blocks.title: 5. Common Pitfalls
blocks.content: The most common trap is applying Theorem 1 (center = 2x circumference) when the two angles are NOT from the same arc! If the angles are looking at different arcs, the theorem doesn't apply. Always trace the arc that both angles are 'looking at'. If they share the same arc, you can use the theorem. If not, look for a different theorem.
